L36: # Dimensions of Fano schemes of lines on hypersurfaces
L37: 
L38: Chenglong Yu
L39: 
L40: ###### Abstract.
L41: 
L42: Let $X\subset\mathbb{P}^{n}_{\mathbb{C}}$ be a smooth hypersurface of degree $d\geq 2$, with $n\geq 3$. We prove that an $m$-dimensional integral projective family of lines sweeping a variety of dimension $y$ satisfies $m\leq\max\{2y-d-1,n-3\}$. This proves the de Jong–Debarre conjecture for $d\leq n$ and the Beheshti–Starr bound for lines on smooth hypersurfaces for $d\geq n+1$.
L43: ## 1. Introduction
L44: 
L45: In this paper, we assume all schemes are of finite type over $\mathbb{C}$ and a variety means an integral separated scheme. Let $X\subset\mathbb{P}^{n}_{\mathbb{C}}$ be a smooth hypersurface of degree $d\geq 2$, with $n\geq 3$. Its Fano scheme of lines $F_{1}(X)\subset\mathrm{Gr}(2,n+1)$ parametrizes lines contained in $X$. It is locally cut out by $d+1$ equations, so every nonempty component has dimension at least $2n-d-3$. In the Fano range, the expected upper bound is the following.
L46: ###### Conjecture 1.1 (de Jong–Debarre [【24†Deb03】, Conjecture 1]).
L47: 
L48: If $d\leq n$, then $\dim F_{1}(X)=2n-d-3$.
L49: 
L50: For higher degrees, the Beheshti–Starr question [【25†Beh05】, Question 1.3], restricted to lines on smooth hypersurfaces, takes the following form [【26†LT10】, p. 574].
L51: ###### Question 1.2 (Beheshti–Starr).
L52: 
L53: If $d\geq n$, does every irreducible component of $F_{1}(X)$ have dimension at most $n-3$?
L54: 
L55: Here $F_{1}(X)$ may be empty. For every $n\geq 3$ and $d\geq n+1$, the classical Fermat example attains the bound $n-3$ [【24†Deb03】, p. 1]. See §【16†5.2】. A stronger statement allowing singular hypersurfaces is formulated in [【26†LT10】, Conjecture 1.1].
L56: For $d\leq n$, Beheshti proves Conjecture 【27†1.1】 in degree at most eight [【28†Beh06】, 【29†Beh14】]. Beheshti–Riedl prove it for $n\geq 2d-4$ using equations for lines through a fixed point and a bound on the dimension of a tangency locus [【30†BR21】, Corollary 2.5]. They also prove irreducibility for $n\geq 2d-1$ and $n\geq 4$ [【30†BR21】, Corollary 2.8]. Landsberg–Tommasi relate both problems to Chern-class nonvanishing on families of lines through a point [【26†LT10】]. We prove the following result.
L57: ###### Theorem 1.3.
L58: 
L59: Let $X\subset\mathbb{P}^{n}_{\mathbb{C}}$ be a smooth hypersurface of degree $d\geq 2$, with $n\geq 3$.
L60: 
L61:   1. (i)
L62: 
L63: If $d\leq n$, then $F_{1}(X)$ is nonempty and every irreducible component has dimension $2n-d-3$.
L64: 
L65:   2. (ii)
L66: 
L67: If $d\geq n+1$, every irreducible component of $F_{1}(X)$ has dimension at most $n-3$.
L68: 
L69: This proves Conjecture 【27†1.1】 and answers Question 【31†1.2】. The main estimate comes from the dimension of the swept variety.
L70: ###### Theorem 1.4.
L71: 
L72: Let $S\subset F_{1}(X)$ be a closed subvariety of dimension $m$, and let $y$ be the dimension of the union of its lines. Then
L73: 
L74: (1)  |  | $$m\leq\max\{2y-d-1,\,n-3\}.$$  |
L75: 
L76: The swept-variety estimate also gives the following consequences. A line $\ell\subset X$ is free if its normal bundle $N_{\ell/X}$ is globally generated.
L77: ###### Corollary 1.5.
L78: 
L79: Let $X\subset\mathbb{P}^{n}_{\mathbb{C}}$ be a smooth hypersurface of degree $d\geq 2$, with $n\geq 3$.
L80: 
L81:   1. (i)
L82: 
L83: If $d\leq n-1$, a general line in every irreducible component of $F_{1}(X)$ is free.
L84: 
L85:   2. (ii)
L86: 
L87: If $d\leq n-2$, then $F_{1}(X)$ is irreducible.
L88: For $d\geq n-2$, every closed subvariety of $F_{1}(X)$ of dimension at least $n-2$ parametrizes lines covering $X$ (Corollary 【32†5.2】). This proves Debarre’s covering conjecture [【24†Deb03】, Conjecture 2]. The Fano scheme is also a local complete intersection for $d\leq n$, reduced for $d\leq n-1$, and normal and integral for $d\leq n-2$ (Corollary 【33†6.4】).
L89: We combine the deformation theory of lines through a fixed point, as in Beheshti–Riedl, with the Chern-class approach of Landsberg–Tommasi. For a family of dimension at least $n-2$, we compare two bounds for the degree of the tautological quotient on the Nash modification along a lifted general line. Deformation theory gives the upper bound. The new step compares determinants up to an effective divisor on a normalized graph closure.
L90: The gradient map and Schubert calculus then give the lower bound $d-1$ for the same degree. This allows singular swept varieties and avoids the tangency-locus dimension bound of [【30†BR21】, Lemma 2.1].
L91: The paper is organized as follows. In §【5†2】–§【9†4】, we establish the line estimate, the numerical quotient inequality, and the determinant comparison. We prove the dimension theorems and Corollaries 【32†5.2】 and 【34†1.5】 in §【14†5】. In §【17†6】, we compare our argument with the earlier methods, derive bounds for nonfree lines, and prove Corollary 【33†6.4】.
L92: ## 2. The Quotient Bundle on the Nash Modification
L93: 
L94: We construct the tautological quotient bundle on the Nash modification of the swept variety and bound its degree along the lift of a line by the dimension of the family.
L95: We use the convention that $\mathbb{P}(E)$ parametrizes one-dimensional subspaces, with $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}(E)}(-1)\subset p^{*}E$. A subbundle has locally free quotient. Degrees of vector bundles on curves mean degrees of determinant bundles or equivalently the degrees of first Chern classes. We use Chern classes as operations on Chow groups and integrate against fundamental cycles [【35†Ful98】].
L96: Let $\mathcal{S}$ be the tautological bundle on $\mathrm{Gr}(2,n+1)$. Restriction of an equation of $X$ realizes $F_{1}(X)$ as the zero scheme of a section of $\mathrm{Sym}^{d}\mathcal{S}^{\vee}$. For a closed subvariety $S\subset F_{1}(X)$, let $p_{S}\colon\mathcal{W}=\mathbb{P}_{S}(\mathcal{S}|_{S})\to S$ be its universal family, with evaluation $e\colon\mathcal{W}\to X$. This is the incidence variety in $S\times X$ defined by $x\in\ell$, with its two projections. Put
L97:  | $$m=\dim S,\qquad Y=e(\mathcal{W})_{\mathrm{red}},\qquad y=\dim Y,\qquad r=n-y,\qquad t=m+1-y.$$  |
L98: 
L99: The projective bundle $\mathcal{W}$ is integral, so its reduced image $Y$ is integral.
L100: Write $V=\mathbb{C}^{n+1}$. For $x\in Y_{\mathrm{sm}}$, let $\widehat{T}_{Y,x}\subset V$ be the $(y+1)$-dimensional vector space whose projectivization is the embedded tangent space. Let $\widehat{Y}$ be the reduced graph closure of $x\mapsto\widehat{T}_{Y,x}$ in $Y\times\mathrm{Gr}(y+1,V)$, with projection $\nu\colon\widehat{Y}\to Y$. This is the projective Gauss-map realization of the classical Nash modification [【36†Nob75】, pp. 297–298]. The tautological sequence is
L101: (2)  |  | $$0\longrightarrow\mathcal{A}_{Y}\longrightarrow V\otimes\mathcal{O}_{\widehat{Y}}\longrightarrow\mathcal{B}_{Y}\longrightarrow 0,\qquad\mathrm{rank}\mathcal{A}_{Y}=y+1,\quad\mathrm{rank}\mathcal{B}_{Y}=r.$$  |
L102: 
L103: Both terms are vector bundles, and $\mathcal{B}_{Y}$ is globally generated.
L104: The partial derivatives of a defining form $F$ of $X$ give the gradient map $V\otimes\mathcal{O}_{Y}\to\mathcal{O}_{Y}(d-1)$, surjective since $X$ is smooth. It annihilates $\widehat{T}_{Y,x}$ because differentiation of $F|_{Y}=0$ gives vanishing on the tangent directions, while Euler’s identity gives vanishing on the radial direction. After pullback, its restriction to $\mathcal{A}_{Y}$ is zero on a dense open set, hence zero on the integral variety $\widehat{Y}$.
L105: Thus it induces an everywhere-surjective map
L106: (3)  |  | $$\mathcal{B}_{Y}\twoheadrightarrow\nu^{*}\mathcal{O}_{Y}(d-1).$$  |
L107: ###### Proposition 2.1.
L108: 
L109: There is a nonempty open $S^{\circ}\subset S_{\mathrm{sm}}$ such that every $\ell=\ell_{s}$, $s\in S^{\circ}$, has a unique lift $\lambda_{\ell}\colon\ell\to\widehat{Y}$, defined on the whole line, with
L110: 
L111: (4)  |  | $$0\leq b_{\ell}:=\deg\lambda_{\ell}^{*}\mathcal{B}_{Y}\leq 2y-m-2.$$  |
L112: ###### Proof.
L113: By generic smoothness, $e$ maps a nonempty open $\Omega\subset p_{S}^{-1}(S_{\mathrm{sm}})$ to $Y_{\mathrm{sm}}$ with differential of rank $y$ [【37†Har77】, III, §10]. Since $p_{S}$ is open, $S^{\circ}=p_{S}(\Omega)$ is nonempty and open. Each line parametrized by $S^{\circ}$ meets $Y_{\mathrm{sm}}$, where $\nu$ is an isomorphism. As $\ell$ is smooth, properness of $\nu$ extends its lift to the whole line, and separatedness gives uniqueness (Lemma 【38†4.1】).
L114: Its image is the strict transform of $\ell$, with no additional components over singular points.
L115: Let $A\subset V$ be the two-dimensional vector subspace defining $\ell$, and put $\mathcal{A}_{\ell}=\lambda_{\ell}^{*}\mathcal{A}_{Y}$ and $\mathcal{B}_{\ell}=\lambda_{\ell}^{*}\mathcal{B}_{Y}$. At a smooth point of $Y$ on $\ell$, its projective tangent space contains the entire line. Hence the map $A\otimes\mathcal{O}_{\ell}\to\mathcal{B}_{\ell}$ is zero generically and therefore everywhere.
L116: The resulting inclusion $A\otimes\mathcal{O}_{\ell}\subset\mathcal{A}_{\ell}$ has constant fiber rank two, so its quotient is locally free. Define
L117:  | $$M_{\ell}=(\mathcal{A}_{\ell}/(A\otimes\mathcal{O}_{\ell}))\otimes\mathcal{O}_{\ell}(1).$$  |
L118: 
L119: Quotienting (【39†2】) by $A\otimes\mathcal{O}_{\ell}$ gives an exact sequence of bundles on the complete line
L120: 
L121: (5)  |  | $$0\longrightarrow M_{\ell}\longrightarrow N_{\ell/\mathbb{P}^{n}}\longrightarrow\mathcal{B}_{\ell}(1)\longrightarrow 0,\qquad N_{\ell/\mathbb{P}^{n}}=(V/A)\otimes\mathcal{O}_{\ell}(1).$$  |
L122: 
L123: In particular $\mathrm{rank}M_{\ell}=y-1$ and $\deg M_{\ell}=y-1-b_{\ell}$.
L124: The differential of $S\hookrightarrow\mathrm{Gr}(2,n+1)$ identifies $T_{s}S$ with a subspace of $H^{0}(N_{\ell/\mathbb{P}^{n}})$. The characteristic map evaluates these sections. For $x\in\Omega\cap\ell$, quotienting the surjective differential $de$ by the fiber direction $T_{x}\ell$ gives $T_{s}S\twoheadrightarrow T_{x}Y/T_{x}\ell=(M_{\ell})_{x}$. The composite with the locally free quotient in (【40†5】) is therefore generically zero, hence everywhere zero.
L125: Thus $T_{s}S$ injects into $H^{0}(M_{\ell})$ and generates $M_{\ell}$ generically.
L126: By Grothendieck’s splitting theorem [【41†Gro57】, Theorem 2.1], we can write $M_{\ell}=\bigoplus_{j}\mathcal{O}_{\ell}(a_{j})$. If $a_{j}<0$, then $H^{0}(\mathcal{O}_{\ell}(a_{j}))=0$, so every global section of $M_{\ell}$ has zero projection to this summand, contradicting generic generation. Hence $a_{j}\geq 0$, and $M_{\ell}$ is generated everywhere by $H^{0}(M_{\ell})$, although the subspace $T_{s}S$ need not generate at every point.
L127: The inclusion into $\mathcal{O}_{\ell}(1)^{n-1}$ also excludes $a_{j}>1$. Therefore
L128: (6)  |  | $$M_{\ell}=\mathcal{O}_{\ell}(1)^{y-1-b_{\ell}}\oplus\mathcal{O}_{\ell}^{b_{\ell}},\qquad m\leq h^{0}(M_{\ell})=2y-2-b_{\ell},$$  |
L129: 
L130: which proves (【42†4】). If $y=1$, $M_{\ell}=0$ and the same injection gives $m=b_{\ell}=0$. ∎
L131: ###### Remark 2.2.
L132: 
L133: For a line $\ell$ meeting $Y_{\mathrm{sm}}$, the normal sheaf $\mathcal{N}_{\ell/Y}=\mathcal{H}om(\mathcal{I}_{\ell/Y}/\mathcal{I}_{\ell/Y}^{2},\mathcal{O}_{\ell})$ satisfies
L134: 
L135:  | $$\mathcal{N}_{\ell/Y}=M_{\ell},\qquad T_{[\ell]}F_{1}(Y)=H^{0}(M_{\ell}).$$  |
L136: Dualizing the conormal sequence of $\ell\subset Y\subset\mathbb{P}^{n}$ shows that $\mathcal{N}_{\ell/Y}$ is saturated in $N_{\ell/\mathbb{P}^{n}}$. It agrees with the saturated subbundle $M_{\ell}$ over $\ell\cap Y_{\mathrm{sm}}$, hence everywhere. The tangent-space identity is Grothendieck’s formula [【43†Gro61】, Corollary 5.3] (see also [【44†AK77】, Proposition 2.16]). For lines as in Proposition 【45†2.1】, (【46†6】) gives $H^{1}(\mathcal{N}_{\ell/Y})=0$.
L137: If $\ell\subset Y$ is not a regular embedding, this vanishing alone does not imply that $F_{1}(Y)$ is smooth at $[\ell]$.
L138: ## 3. Schubert Calculus and a Quotient Inequality
L139: 
L140: We prove a numerical inequality for a globally generated bundle with a line-bundle quotient. The proof uses Chern operations on Chow homology, their compatibility with proper pushforward, and Whitney’s formula over an arbitrary base [【35†Ful98】, Chapter 3]. See also [【47†Stacks】, Tags 【48†02U4†stacks.math.columbia.edu】 and 【49†02UI†stacks.math.columbia.edu】].
L141: ### 3.1. Nonnegativity on Singular Cycles
L142: 
L143: We record a standard consequence of Schubert calculus and Kleiman’s transversality theorem.
L144: ###### Lemma 3.1.
L145: 
L146: Let $E$ be a globally generated vector bundle of rank $r\geq 1$ on a projective scheme $Q$, and let $L$ be a globally generated line bundle on $Q$. For an effective $q$-cycle $\alpha$ on $Q$, one has
L147:  | $\displaystyle\deg\bigl(c_{i}(E)c_{1}(L)^{q-i}\cap\alpha\bigr)$  | $\displaystyle\geq 0$  |  | $\displaystyle(0\leq i\leq\min\{r,q\}),$  |
L148:  | $\displaystyle\deg\bigl((c_{1}(E)c_{i}(E)-c_{i+1}(E))c_{1}(L)^{q-i-1}\cap\alpha\bigr)$  | $\displaystyle\geq 0$  |  | $\displaystyle(1\leq i\leq r,\ i+1\leq q).$  |
L149: 
L150: Here $c_{r+1}(E)=0$. Neither smoothness nor normality of the cycle supports, nor reducedness of $Q$, is assumed.
L151: ###### Proof.
L152: 
L153: Choose a generating map $\mathbb{C}^{N}\otimes\mathcal{O}_{Q}\twoheadrightarrow E$. It defines $f\colon Q\to\mathrm{Gr}(N-r,N)$ with $E=f^{*}\mathcal{Q}$, where $\mathcal{Q}$ is the universal rank-$r$ quotient. By adjoining zero sections, we may assume that $s=N-r\geq 2$. A generating space for $L$ similarly defines $\psi\colon Q\to\mathbb{P}^{M}$ with $L=\psi^{*}\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{P}^{M}}(1)$. Write $\Phi=(f,\psi)$.
L154: We recall the convention for Schubert classes used here. For a complete flag $F_{\bullet}$ in $\mathbb{C}^{N}$ and a partition $\lambda$ with at most $s$ parts, each at most $r$, let
L155:
